title: Cambodian Remake of Korean Mother-Daughter Drama ‘Wedding Dress’ Leads Abnormal Studios’ Busan Market Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A Phnom Penh-set reworking of Kwon Hyung-jin’s 2010 South Korean drama “Wedding Dress” is the lead title for Malaysia’s Abnormal Studios at this yea
body:
A Phnom Penh-set reworking of Kwon Hyung-jin’s 2010 South Korean drama “Wedding Dress” is the lead title for Malaysia’s Abnormal Studios at this year’s Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, where the company is selling the film ahead of its local release.

	The new version centers on Dalin, a single mother who designs bridal gowns and whose devotion to her job has opened a gap between her and her 10-year-old daughter Mina. A terminal diagnosis shifts her priorities, and she sets about readying everything she thinks the girl will need for a happy life once she has died.
	

	The Cambodian adaptation is the first feature from Huang Han, whose earlier work has screened at the Berlin, Busan and Pingyao film festivals. It keeps the core of the mother-daughter story while anchoring it in the day-to-day life and emotional textures of the region.


	Also on the slate is “The Hungry One,” Venezuelan horror director Alejandro Hidalgo’s upcoming feature. His credits include “No Voltees” (2024); “The Exorcism of God” (2021), which was distributed in more than 150 countries; and his 2013 breakout “The House at the End of Time,” Venezuela’s top-grossing horror film.

	The story follows Emily, a white American woman whose Chinese husband takes her to visit his relatives’ ancestral home in Malaysia over the 15-day Hungry Ghost Festival, when the boundary with the underworld is lifted and ghosts wander among the living. A mounting series of eerie encounters puts everything she cares about at risk.

	The film is in pre-production, and its producers are working to close the last round of financing.
	

	The company is also handling “Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,” an independent cannibal black comedy-horror from Feisal and Iskander Azizuddin. In it, two friends with nothing to lose become hooked on power after hitting on a winning spicy beef jerky recipe made with human flesh.

	From Malaysia comes sci-fi fantasy “Mimpi Kita: Castle in the Air,” which pits a simulated world against a dystopian real one as it asks what children owe their parents. The project took part in the It Project section of the NAFF Project Market at Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival this year.

	The wider pan-Asian lineup features “Because of You Ka Kui,” a film celebrating Canto rock frontman Wong Ka Kui which, according to the company, has drawn strong fan support in select territories, and “Next Stop, Somewhere,” a drama led by Hong Kong veteran Anthony Wong. From Cambodia comes fish-out-of-water rom-com “Far Away Close to You,” which plays on the might-have-beens of youthful romance.

	Other Southeast Asian titles are “The Ghost of Banana Tree,” adapted from a well-known Cambodian folk horror legend; “Silent Murders,” a crime thriller set in Cambodia’s criminal underworld; “KL Love Story,” an ensemble drama about temptation, loyalty and loneliness in Kuala Lumpur’s after-dark scene; and supernatural horror “Her Deadly Eyes.”

	Indonesian audience favorites round things out, among them the horror franchises “The Doll,” “Mata Batin” and “Rumah Kentang,” and the rom-coms “Sunshine Becomes You” and the “Eiffel… I’m in Love” series.

	Abnormal Studios, a subsidiary of Westec Media Limited, has been acquiring and releasing films since 2020 and has handled more than 400 titles to date. It now puts out around 100 films a year across Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Mongolia and Nepal, with recent hits including “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and “Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.”

schema.headline: Cambodian Remake of Korean Mother-Daughter Drama ‘Wedding Dress’ Leads Abnormal Studios’ Busan Market Slate (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Michael Douglas Tells Bill Maher About Smuggling Marijuana in Suitcases, Slams ‘Nepo Baby’ Label
description: On Friday night, Michael Douglas stopped by “Real Time with Bill Maher” to promote his mammoth memoir “One Helluva Ride,” chronicling the acclaimed
body:
On Friday night, Michael Douglas stopped by “Real Time with Bill Maher” to promote his mammoth memoir “One Helluva Ride,” chronicling the acclaimed actor and producer’s rise through the Hollywood ranks, from winning the Best Picture Oscar for producing “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” to winning the Best Actor Oscar for “Wall Street” to the present-day.

	The book also covered “sex, drugs and rock and roll,” as he told Maher, including how Douglas helped pay for college by smuggling marijuana across the country in fancy suitcases gifted to him by his actor-father Kirk Douglas.
	

	“You and I share something in common about getting through college together,” offered Douglas, to which Maher replied, “What it is we discovered is that when you buy pot in one place and sell it in a different place, the difference between those two amounts can be very good in living your life.”

	“Especially between East Coast and West Coast,” Douglas added. “When I turned 21, Dad wrote me a check for $10,000 and said, ‘Great son, you’re on your own.’ I said, ‘Well, Dad, this is wonderful, but I’ve got a couple of years of tuition left in school…’”

	So, Douglas took matters into his own hands. “One time I said, ‘Dad, you remember one Christmas you bought me two beautiful Italian soft leather suitcases? Well, I found out that each one of those suitcases could hold 22 kilos of marijuana.’ I would go back east to see my mom with the clothes on my back and two suitcases. This was called BD: Before Dogs.”

	Later on in their talk, the HBO host gave Douglas props for working normal jobs to make money despite having a rich actor as a father, including his time working at a Mobil gas station in Connecticut at the age of 20 and earning the title of “Mobil Man of the Month.” The topic prompted Douglas to address the “nepo baby” discourse, where the children of Hollywood players have been criticized for getting a significant leg up in the industry.
	

	“With this ‘nepo baby’ thing, doesn’t every single business, doesn’t a father or a mother want their son or daughter to go into the business?” he asked, defensively. “They have a sign that says ‘so and so and sons,’ so why pick on show business?”

schema.headline: Michael Douglas Tells Bill Maher About Smuggling Marijuana in Suitcases, Slams ‘Nepo Baby’ Label

title: ‘Exorcism of God’ Director Alejandro Hidalgo to Helm Malaysian Hungry Ghost Festival Horror ‘The Hungry One’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Alejandro Hidalgo, director of “The Exorcism of God,” is set to make “The Hungry One,” a supernatural horror film unfolding over Malaysia’s Hungry G
body:
Alejandro Hidalgo, director of “The Exorcism of God,” is set to make “The Hungry One,” a supernatural horror film unfolding over Malaysia’s Hungry Ghost Festival.

	Kuala Lumpur-based Abnormal Studios is handling worldwide sales and is introducing the project at the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market. Singapore-based Clover Films has already picked up rights for Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
	

	The story follows Emily, an American woman who travels with Simon, her Chinese Malaysian husband, and their son Louis to spend the summer at his family’s mansion. Their stay coincides with the 15-day festival, when the underworld is believed to open and the dead mingle with the living. Emily becomes the target of escalating encounters with a vengeful presence trying to cross over, and must dig into the house’s hidden past before it takes her family.


	Filmmaker and entrepreneur Justin Leong is driving the project through Los Angeles-based Lightning Pictures.

	“Growing up in Asia, I always felt the Hungry Ghost Festival was incredibly rich visually, from the fire and offerings to the rituals and mythology behind it. When you capture that and shoot it cinematically, it’s movie gold. It gives us a world that audiences may not have seen before, but one that feels immediately atmospheric, mysterious and made for horror,” Leong said.

	Leong, who has deep ties to Malaysian-Chinese culture, drew on his own family’s traditions to shape the story.

	Hidalgo’s first feature, “The House at the End of Time,” remains Venezuela’s biggest horror hit at the box office. It earned strong notices on the festival circuit and has since gathered a cult audience for mixing the supernatural with science fiction. His 2021 follow-up, “The Exorcism of God,” bowed at Fantastic Fest and went on to sell to more than 150 countries, with Saban Films handling its U.S. theatrical release. It ended 2022 as the highest-grossing Latin American film worldwide.
	

	Producer Harrison Allen, who won the live action short Oscar at this year’s Academy Awards for Netflix title “The Singers,” is also on board. His latest feature, “Anima,” screened at SXSW this year. 

	Also attached is Thomas Percy Kim, a Sundance and Toronto fellow whose debut feature “Isle Child,” based on his own short that HBO Max acquired, premiered in Toronto. Screenwriter Justin Parker worked on the development of HBO’s Emmy-nominated limited series “Station Eleven” and was a writer on docuseries “Religion of Sports.”

	“The Hungry One” is in pre-production, with its producers working to lock the last portion of its financing.

	Abnormal Studios, a subsidiary of Westec Media Limited, has been acquiring and releasing films since 2020 and has handled more than 400 titles to date. It now brings around 100 films a year to Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Mongolia and Nepal. Recent releases include “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and “Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.”

schema.headline: ‘Exorcism of God’ Director Alejandro Hidalgo to Helm Malaysian Hungry Ghost Festival Horror ‘The Hungry One’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Danny Trejo Speaks Out About His Role in Daily Wire ‘Pawn Shop’ Movie: ‘I Am Not Pro-ICE. I Am Pro-Immigrant.’
description: Danny Trejo has issued his first statement since facing backlash for starring in the pro-ICE Daily Wire movie “Pawn Shop” from Ben Shapiro‘s product
body:
Danny Trejo has issued his first statement since facing backlash for starring in the pro-ICE Daily Wire movie “Pawn Shop” from Ben Shapiro‘s production company. 

	“I am a proud Mexican who has always been and will always be a supporter of my community. I am also obviously pro-immigrant. I am not pro-ICE,” the “Spy Kids” actor told TMZ.

	“I know where I come from and I know our struggles,” he added, “I am an actor. My job is to tell a story.” TMZ reported that Trejo had told people on set that he was attracted to the role because it was a positive depiction of a Latino who is also a veteran. 
	

	The production was shut down in Livingston, Montana last Saturday when locals complained about the production’s impact on the Livingston food bank and improper warnings about hazardous stunts. Production resumed Monday, with political commentator Shapiro slamming the shutdown as  “content discrimination” and “a violation of the First Amendment.”

	One scene that was captured on video by TMZ appeared to recreate the fatal ICE shooting of Renee Good. Harvey Keitel co-stars as a fellow veteran hired by Trejo’s character to work at the pawn shop.

	The logline for the film reads: “When a Minneapolis riot forces a young ICE officer to complete a high-stakes arrest alone after his partner is killed, he is hunted through the streets by a furious mob intent on freeing the prisoner and punishing anyone who still upholds the law. Barricaded inside a neighborhood pawn shop with a hard-edged Hispanic veteran and the man’s progressive college-age grandson, ordinary men must choose between the rule of law and the chaos that wants to burn it all down in a modern siege of honor and defiance.”
	

	Trejo’s rep confirmed his statements but had no further comment.

schema.headline: Danny Trejo Speaks Out About His Role in Daily Wire ‘Pawn Shop’ Movie: ‘I Am Not Pro-ICE. I Am Pro-Immigrant.’

title: Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC
description: Jason Blum and James Wan aren’t paying much attention to the bad reviews (but massive box office success!) for “Other Mommy.” Instead, the horror ma
body:
Jason Blum and James Wan aren’t paying much attention to the bad reviews (but massive box office success!) for “Other Mommy.” Instead, the horror maestros spent Friday night looking ahead at what’s next, unveiling Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s upcoming slate of films during the 90-minute presentation at New York Comic Con.

	In the next year, the horror house will launch a new installment of the “Exorcist” franchise starring Scarlett Johansson, “Violent Night 2” with Kristen Bell, and a revamped “Blair Witch Project.”
	

	During the event, Blumhouse announced a new short-film deal with Heidi Wong, a MatPat-led adaptation of the indie video game “Amanda the Adventurer,” and Oscar nominee LaKeith Stanfield’s next movie, “Molepeople.”


	If you couldn’t make it to the horror-filled presentation, read below for more of the major takeaways from the Blumhouse panel at NYCC.

	Jason Blum Addresses the Doppelganger Elephant In The Room

	Despite its major box office success, “Other Mommy” debuted this weekend to an onslaught of negative reviews. One of the things that was picked apart online was the title of the film itself, particularly why it wasn’t named “Other Mother” both for the sake of the rhyme and to further the parallels between “Coraline.”

	“Well, funnily enough, my partner James Wan wanted to call it ‘Other Mother,’ and he got outvoted,” Blum revealed during the panel. “This is probably why we should always listen to James Wan.”

	Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ As Mrs. Clause

	Kristen Bell is getting into the Christmas spirit, and no, it isn’t with “Frozen.”
	

	The actress is joining David Harbour in “Violent Night 2,” stepping into the jolly-but-deadly shoes of Mrs. Claus.

	“It was thrilling to get this call from David. I think I was so confused when he called, because I didn’t even know they were making a second one,” Bell said during the panel. “David called and said, ‘I need you to come to Winnipeg.’ And I was like, ‘What? No.’”

	As a big fan of the first film, Bell shared that once she learned it was for “Violent Night 2,” she was in. She revealed David told her she would play Mrs. Claus, who is a “‘badass and she’s every bit as capable as Santa is.’ And I said, ‘Say more.’ And we made it work.”

	‘Paranormal Activity,’ ‘Blair Witch’ and ‘Saw 11’ Teased

	The fan-favorite film “Paranormal Activity” is getting a modern makeover and is set to release in theaters May 21, coming alongside the news of the Broadway play’s extension into February.

	“’Paranormal Activity’ is such an emotional movie for me, because it’s really how Blumhouse started,” Blum shared. “It really gave birth to everything that we’ve done.”

	Wan and Blum announced the news with a teaser video of director Ian Tuason reenacting the infamous at-home footage of becoming possessed while sleeping overnight before turning to the camera to share the film is currently in production.

	For the new take on “The Blair Witch Project,” Wan said he’s “super excited” about director Dylan Clark. “Dylan is another one of these great filmmakers, YouTubers who’ve made a bunch of really great shorts online … It’s these filmmakers who actually have a lot of reverence for these films. They grew up with it, and they have a lot of admiration for it. And so we’re not just plucking anyone off the internet.”

	Blum joined Wan on stage again to discuss the upcoming 11th “Saw” film, which will be directed by Mike P. Nelson. The film had been in development limbo for several years but is now back on track after the Blumhouse-Atomic Monster merger. 

	“I said, if you and Leigh Whannell are going to come back to do this, I want to make sure that you’re in the driver’s seat for how it’s going to go creatively,” Blum said. “It’s going to feel, I think, different than every other every other ‘Saw’ movie before, maybe except the first, which James obviously directed and wrote with Leigh. And on both of our parts, we want to thank you guys for keeping that franchise alive for all these years and we’re gonna bring it to you in a whole new way. So with James and Lee coming back, and all of your love for Saw, it was time to bring it home.”
	

	Craig Zobel Is Directing Adaptation of Comic Book Horror ‘Something Is Killing the Children’

	Director Craig Zobel announced he will direct the adaptation of James Tynion IV and Werther Dell’Edera’s “Something Is Killing the Children.”

	Blumhouse is developing the franchise both as a live-action film and an adult animated television series, with Tynion IV spearheading the latter. Stephen Christy and James Tynion IV will produce the film for BOOM! Studios and Penguin Random House, alongside Jason Blum for Blumhouse. Shaun Sutton, Ryan Turek, Adam Yoelin and Mette Norkjaer will executive produce. Dell’Edera will as co-produce.

	Blumhouse Is Making More Than Just Movies

	And TV shows. The production company’s horror game, “Grave Seasons,” is officially launching March 9, following a couple years of teasing the game’s arrival. Blum shared they will also share prize packs that include Fortnite codes that celebrate the Purge’s Lady Liberty as part of Fortnightmares.

schema.headline: Jason Blum on How ‘Other Mommy’ Got That Controversial Title, Kristen Bell Joins ‘Violent Night 2’ and More From Blumhouse at NYCC

title: ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Producer Backs Park Syeyoung’s Memory-Bending Love Motel Drama ‘Satellite of Love’ at Busan Asian Project Market
description: A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging
body:
A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging her love life all along in “Satellite of Love,” the fourth feature from South Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung (“The Fin”). 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).


	The motel sits among reed beds and woods, its rooms echoing with lovers every night. When her lover walks out, the woman insists he come back in 10 years, to the day and the hour. He says no. She stays put regardless, never leaving the room and cycling through the same chores – eating, washing up, laundering the sheets – while guests check in and out around her.
	

	A decade on, a man turns up saying he is the one who left. She doesn’t know his face, but he keeps at it, and slowly they fall in love. Then the cracks show. Their conversations start to loop. When he pleads with her to run away with him, the motel’s managers take him away.

	The truth is that the motel exists to keep the woman’s feelings alive and replay them. Men brought in from outside are coached to act out romances with her again and again, performing love, regret and guilt while their tears are gathered. Once she knows this, she goes back to her routine and turns her eyes to the door, waiting again for someone to come back.

	“I hope to convey the way in which our memories are so volatile and how the present can keep altering what has happened in the past,” Park says. “How nothing is definite and every memory is subject to change.”
	

	Park has been working on his third feature, “Who Stole My Cross?,” which is now in post-production. His first two features followed groups of characters from the outside, without digging into their inner wants, while “Who Stole My Cross?” centers on a single figure. That shift pushed him further, and he wants “Satellite of Love” to be driven entirely by its character. The script is in development.

	The film is produced by Coproduction Office’s Philippe Bober and creative producer Sylvain Cruiziat. The company has worked with Park on “The Masked Monster” and “The Fin,” which played Locarno in 2024 and 2025, respectively, and on “Who Stole My Cross?” Bober, who founded the company, produced Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or winners “Triangle of Sadness” and “The Square.” 

	The producers rank Park as a singular voice in present-day Korean cinema. “Satellite of Love” will be their fourth film together. “We are thrilled to continue supporting Syeyoung on his path as an auteur, and to accompany him on this next chapter,” they say.

	At the APM, the team wants to meet potential Asian co-production partners and financiers and to put Park’s next film in front of the industry early.

	Beyond “Satellite of Love,” Park is writing several commercial features he hopes to shoot in Korea alongside more personal projects he will make independently. “I will make films till I die, and I want to explore a range of financing approaches along the way,” he says.

schema.headline: ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Producer Backs Park Syeyoung’s Memory-Bending Love Motel Drama ‘Satellite of Love’ at Busan Asian Project Market

title: Edward Zhang, Casper Van Dien, Jeff Fahey Star in China-U.S. WWII Spy Series ‘Operation Doolittle,’ Heading to Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE)
description: World War II espionage drama “Operation Doolittle,” a China-U.S. co-production starring Edward Zhang, Casper Van Dien and Jeff Fahey, is heading to
body:
World War II espionage drama “Operation Doolittle,” a China-U.S. co-production starring Edward Zhang, Casper Van Dien and Jeff Fahey, is heading to the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market, where Cappu Films is presenting it to buyers as worldwide sales agent.

	The nine-part series, made up of 60-minute episodes, also stars Ning Chang (“Girls,” “The Soul”). Zhang’s credits include “Legend of the Demon Cat,” Van Dien’s include “Starship Troopers” and “Sleepy Hollow,” and Fahey has appeared in “Alita: Battle Angel” and “Lost.”
	

	The show spins a fictional intelligence story around the Doolittle Raid of 1942. It opens as an American intelligence officer, carrying secret plans for the bombing, is downed over a Japanese-occupied island near China’s southern coast. A Chinese agent working undercover inside the Japanese army teams up with a local military doctor to retrieve the plans, shield the operation and clear the way for Doolittle and his airmen to reach China.


	Characters speak English, Chinese and Japanese. The drama mixes battlefield action with a tale of conflicted allegiances and the dangers of undercover work in hostile territory.

	Zhao Jun, a longtime Chinese TV writer and producer, penned the series. Directing duties are shared by China’s Zhao Yilong and American filmmaker Shaun Piccinino. Chinese stars Morning Chang and Zhang Songwen round out the ensemble, and Han Sanping, who previously ran China Film Group, serves as executive producer.

	The show debuted on Chinese screens as “River Sunset” (“Chang He Luo Ri”) earlier this year. It was later recut into the nine-episode “Operation Doolittle” for viewers outside the country.
	

	“‘Operation Doolittle’ brings to life one of the most daring missions of World War II – the Doolittle Raid – and tells it from both Chinese and American perspectives. At its heart is a remarkable story of two countries coming together in wartime,” said Zhao. “We hope the series not only brings this shared history to a global audience, but also opens the door to a new generation of China-U.S. co-productions.”

	Janice Woo of Cappu Films added: “Its story of courage and trust across divided loyalties, together with its international cast, gives us much to share with broadcasters and platforms. We look forward to working with the producers to help the series reach audiences around the world.” 

	Cappu’s Busan lineup also features “Fox Hunt,” toplined by Tony Leung Chiu-wai; Shan Jiang’s “Ephemera,” a Tribeca selection; Erica Xia-Hou’s Slamdance title “Banr”; martial arts film “Lion Fist”; Joy Hopwood’s Australian dramedy “Her Last Laugh”; and action comedy “Zombie Plane,” starring Vanilla Ice, Sophie Monk and Chuck Norris.

schema.headline: Edward Zhang, Casper Van Dien, Jeff Fahey Star in China-U.S. WWII Spy Series ‘Operation Doolittle,’ Heading to Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Magic: The Gathering Reveals New ‘Darkhold Destiny’ Marvel Set, ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Theater-Only Card Giveaway
description: Magic: The Gathering has unveiled its next Marvel-themed set and announced a special collaboration with the upcoming theatrical release of “Avengers
body:
Magic: The Gathering has unveiled its next Marvel-themed set and announced a special collaboration with the upcoming theatrical release of “Avengers: Doomsday.”

	Titled “Darkhold Destiny,” the set is focused on “the mystical, the mythical and the mighty” magical characters from the Marvel universe, including Doctor Strange, Thor, Hela and Dormammu. The collection, which marks the third “Universes Beyond” collaboration in Magic and Marvel’s multiyear deal, will include a brand-new storyline set in the Marvel Universe and an original character created by the team.
	

	The “Darkhold Destiny” Magic set will release April 7, 2027 and debut alongside a new Marvel comic book that showcases the story.


	“This is a new kind of Universes Beyond set,” reads the description from Hasbro’s Wizards of the Coast, the makers of Magic: The Gathering. “By taking the core elements players love about Magic: The Gathering, the team thoughtfully and strategically expressed those design intentions through the Marvel Universe. The narrative unfolds across nearly 30 dimensions and is centered around four main characters — Doctor Strange, Thor, Hela and Dormammu.”

	The news was revealed during Magic’s New York Comic Con panel Friday, where Wizards also announced that fans who see “Avengers: Doomsday” opening weekend in Infinity Vision at Regal Cinemas will receive an exclusive Magic: The Gathering card featuring Doctor Doom.

	Additionally, two more Marvel-Magic team-ups were promoted during the panel: a special release called “Doomsdrop” and a new Secret Lair kit titled “Marvel’s History of Heroes.”
	

	The Doomsdrop is inspired by the Marvel comics and is a multi-drop collection that will “predominantly feature Doctor Doom, although fans should expect other special guests from the Marvel Universe,” according to Wizards.

	“Secret Lair Countdown Kit: Marvel’s History of Heroes” is a collection of 30 cards “that bring the storied past of Marvel to life.” That limited-edition drop will launch Nov. 2 at 9 a.m. PT and is priced at $199.99.

	Per Wizards, “The release features illustrations crafted by over 30 artists celebrating iconic moments from Marvel’s comic history — from the transformation of the Fantastic Four in space via cosmic rays, to the first appearance of Iron Man with Ho Yinsen, to Jean Grey’s transformation into the fiery Phoenix.”

	See below for a first look at cards from the new “Darkhold Destiny” Magic: The Gathering set.

schema.headline: Magic: The Gathering Reveals New ‘Darkhold Destiny’ Marvel Set, ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Theater-Only Card Giveaway

title: ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay’s Powerful Sequel to ‘13th’ Turns a Constitutional Amendment into Living History
description: It’s rare to see a dramatic feature filmmaker move into the realm of documentary with the craftmanship and authority and insightful power summoned b
body:
It’s rare to see a dramatic feature filmmaker move into the realm of documentary with the craftmanship and authority and insightful power summoned by Ava DuVernay. “13th,” the documentary she made back in 2016, was a revelation — it told the lacerating story of how the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, which abolished slavery, was a revolutionary act of law that, at the same time, opened the door to the way that numerous dimensions of slavery would be perpetuated in America under different names and tactics. The film was despairing and inspiring in equal measure; it cleansed you with the truth.
	

	Tonight, the New York Film Festival presented the premiere of “14th,” a documentary follow-up in which DuVernay sets her sights on the 14th Amendment, a Constitutional addendum, ratified in 1868, that was so monumental — it guarantees equal protection under the law, but also encompasses five intricate sections that deal with issues from insurrection to due process — that one observer calls it “a Constitution in and of itself,” and another hails it as “the everything bagel of democracy.”


	“14th,” I’m pleased to report, exerts the same kind of historical/topical force that “13th” did. DuVernay, while she works in an extremely accessible and mainstream way, has a singular gift for making the nuances of history come alive. “14th” is steeped in history, but it’s not a dry lecture. Instead, DuVernay cuts through the dusty complacency with which we tend to regard the Constitution (just hearing that word can make you feel like you’re back in school) and shows you that the Constitution is a living, breathing document, one that we fail to heed at our peril. Which is more or less what’s happening today.
	

	A potent movie about history almost has to surprise you. It needs to show you that what you think you know isn’t the half of it. “14th” kicks off with the cutting insight that the three amendments to the Constitution that were passed in the aftermath of the Civil War — the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments — represented nothing less than a restart of American life and society. Yet we don’t necessarily talk about them that way. Everyone knows who “the framers” of the Constitution were (Hamilton, Jefferson, Franklin), but “14th” argues that the period just after the cataclysm of the Civil War had its own framers, who were nearly as significant. Thaddeus Stevens, a member of the House of Representatives who was part of the Radical Republican faction of the 1860s, is a figure who, according to one of the film’s observers, “created the world we live in today.”

	With the abolition of slavery, four million people who were formerly enslaved were suddenly added to the fabric of American society. How would that work? DuVernay tell the story of Reconstruction through fresh eyes, and part of the power of her chronicle is that she doesn’t stint on the joy and liberation that were part of it. Black Americans, who were now citizens, formed communities and industries, they became newspaper editors and law enforcers, as well as politicians (there were 1,000 newly elected Black representatives). But it’s more than that. The point is made that Black people, for the first time in American life, could create a fully realized dream of who they wanted to be as individuals. But this would not work unless their citizenship was enshrined. That’s the first thing the 14th Amendment did. It guaranteed equal protection under the law, and it established birthright citizenship for all people born in the United States — a radical idea, one designed to apply to both the children of former enslaved people and the children of immigrants, because what that represented was a stepping up of the rejection of the European aristocratic system (i.e., citizenship by legacy) that had first been overthrown by the American Revolution. Birthright citizenship continued what the original Constitution started.

	In recent years, it’s become a stylistic tic in documentaries to keep the talking heads offscreen, letting their words simply flow on the soundtrack without interrupting the images. DuVernay is having none of that. She has assembled an extraordinary roster of scholars, politicians, and commentators, led by the Civil Rights attorney Sherrilyn Ifill, who becomes the film’s oratorical star. We see the speakers and absorb the play of their personalities, as they describe, with a big-picture yet highly personalized passion, how the law of the land actually played out in the creation of the second America that rose from the ashes of the Civil War. DuVernay makes history organic by capturing how the very texture of people’s lives was changed by the law. And she’ll go wherever she needs to illustrate that, even to comedy clips from George Carlin and the great Paul Mooney, who does a bit about the happiness of white people when they were slave owners that must be seen to be believed. (His bit isn’t really about the slave era; it’s about today.)
	

	As the film captures, the rise of the new Black citizenry during Reconstruction was rapid. For one thing, Black Americans did not waste time or spirit on vengeance. But the fall was every bit as rapid, as a culture of systematized violence and murder rose up in the South to try to stuff the genie of emancipation back in the bottle. The Ku Klux Klan was one half of it. The other half is captured in DuVernay’s fascinating portrait of the Lost Cause — the culture of defiance and regret and literal whitewashing that came to represent the Southern consciousness of what life had been before the Civil War. Slavery itself, the obscene horror and inhumanity of it, was washed out of the collective memory, and the Civil War was recast as “the war of Northern aggression.”

	What remained were totems and symbols that were somehow infused with nobility. The film traces the history of the Confederate flag as signifier, showing us how rock stars from Tom Petty to ZZ Top used it as a badass backdrop, and spotlighting how the flag was imprinted on the roof of the General Lee, the orange 1969 Dodge Charger driven by the heroes of “The Dukes of Hazzard.” This was one of the most popular TV shows of its time (it debuted in 1979, just as Jimmy Carter’s presidency was winding down), and it was basically using the semiotics of the Civil War — of those who went to war to maintain slavery — as a signifier of cool.

	This consciousness extended to the erecting of Confederate monuments in public squares, a movement so widespread — there were 2,629 such monuments built across the South — that it became larger than the sum of its parts. The message to Black citizens, according to one the film’s observers, was, “You matter so little that we’ll celebrate the people who wanted to enslave you.” The film looks at what the movement to remove those monuments, notably the statue of Robert E. Lee that stood in the capital of Virginia (the former capital of the Confederacy), was really about and what it entailed. It’s all part of how the Lost Cause myth became what the film calls “the greatest lie in American history.”

	But what does that have to do with the 14th Amendment? DuVernay is getting to that. The true subject of the movie is the power of law, and the erosion of law. The dehumanization of Black people represented by the persistence of Confederate iconography in mainstream culture became an underground signifier of the precariousness of the freedoms enshrined by the 14th Amendment. The rise of the Klan, who took their cross-burning imagery from “The Birth of a Nation” (1915), wasn’t simply a matter of domestic terrorism. It was an attempt “to overthrow biracial democracy.” Between the Civil War and World War II, there were 4,400 lynchings. So entrenched was the backlash against Reconstruction, which was institutionalized with Jim Crow (a system of “law” that was really a culture of fascist violence), that it wasn’t until Brown vs. Board of Education, in 1954, that the might of the 14th Amendment began to reassert itself.
	

	Documentaries tend to lessen in impact when they catch up to recent events, but as “14th” moves into the current era something remarkable happens: The film’s themes of racial oppression begin to mutate into themes of generalized oppression. The section of the 14th Amendment that deals with “insurrection” could not be more explicit. It states that anyone who has been responsible for fomenting an insurrection against the United States government cannot run for public office. This means that Donald Trump, after the unambiguous insurrection of Jan. 6, should not have been allowed to run for president in 2024. In that sense, he trampled on the Constitution simply by being re-elected, and the trashing of the 14th Amendment continued unabated. Birthright citizenship? Ignored. Due process? Out the window with ICE.

	The degree to which the United States has been in the ugly thick of a Constitutional crisis since the beginning of 2025 has been persistently understated by the media. But Ava DuVernay states it with meticulous boldness. I don’t agree with her attempt to posit DEI as a Constitutional issue on the level of the Voting Rights Act. (The film itself acknowledges that the DEI movement, whatever one’s opinion of it, represented nothing so much as a “cultural shift.”) But where she shows us the big picture is in capturing how the freedoms of the 14th Amendment have been under siege, and how this may be nothing less than the ritual growing pains — the built-in trauma — of American democracy. Advance, backlash, conflict spilling over into violence…and then re-advance. That’s the rhythm, the moral and spiritual roller-coaster of perfecting our imperfect union. “14th” makes you see that we’re in the heat of the backlash now. But it also lets you feel that a re-advance is waiting in the wings.

schema.headline: ‘14th’ Review: Ava DuVernay’s Powerful Sequel to ‘13th’ Turns a Constitutional Amendment into Living History

title: Bill Burr on ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Sparring With Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg and Why Tech CEOs are ‘Leading Us to Ruin’
description: Over three decades in stand-up comedy, Bill Burr has gained a reputation for saying, with gruff conviction and political fire, the thing on everyone
body:
Over three decades in stand-up comedy, Bill Burr has gained a reputation for saying, with gruff conviction and political fire, the thing on everyone’s mind. In Aaron Sorkin’s new film “The Social Reckoning,” Burr gets to aim that unfiltered attitude at Mark Zuckerberg.

	Burr plays Charlie Garrigan in the follow-up to “The Social Network,” which follows the Facebook founder during the pandemic, as an investigative journalist threatens to lay bare his company’s misdeeds while Zuckerberg, played by Jeremy Strong, grapples with his own role in fueling the Jan. 6 Capitol insurrection. Charlie, a Facebook investor-turned-critic, fictionalized for the film, shows the tech titan tough love as he helps him prepare to testify before Congress.
	

	Burr was offered the part after Sorkin saw him in David Mamet’s Broadway production of “Glengarry Glen Ross,” in which the comic played angry salesman Dave Moss. Shortly after that performance, Burr received a call from his agent: Sorkin wanted to pitch him a movie role.


	“I thought that was hilarious, because it’s like, ‘Dude, you’re Aaron Sorkin. I’d put up staging in the background with no lines to be in a movie that you’re doing,’” Burr says. “He was so humble, and he was taking the time to pitch me the role like I’m somebody. It made me feel good.”
	
		Your character is fictional, or an amalgamation of figures from Zuckerberg’s past. Was it freeing to not have to tie your performance to a real person, or did that make things more challenging?	

	It eliminated the steps of me having to try to become a specific person. Although, I have to tell you, I’m still trying to get better at acting, so I would have been up for it if that was on the table. With Charlie and Zuckerberg, so much going on between these two guys. There’s a business relationship, a friendship, a falling out. I’m catching him in the crosshairs right before he goes in front of Congress, and half of the room is just teaching him how to talk to Congress so he doesn’t have to change the damage that he’s doing.
	

	I get to say the thing that everybody is talking around, which is a very stand-up thing. So much of comedy is you just say the thing, and then it releases all of this tension. But unlike a comedy show like I do, where I’m just messing around, this is legit. This is a big problem that Facebook had. So it was definitely challenging in a really fun way.
	
		What was it like acting opposite Jeremy Strong? I imagine his process is unlike some of the scene partners you’ve had in the past.	

	Well, everybody’s process is different, so it was just working across from another actor that had a different process. But we were all thrown in there together, and it was interesting because we worked six days in a row, so it really felt like we were doing the thing that [Zuckerberg and the crisis PR team] was doing.
	
		Had you met “Jeremy” before the movie wrapped, or were you only dealing with “Zuckerberg”?	

	I had gone to a Broadway play he did, “An Enemy of the People,” and met him there. But that whole mystique around [Method acting] — you know, they’re playing Winnie the Pooh and they were Winnie the Pooh the whole time. Was that weird? I mean, I don’t need to be playing hacky sack with somebody in between takes. Some people are gregarious and they shoot the breeze with you right up until they say their lines. Other people get quiet. Other people go talk to a wall. At this point, I’ve been doing it long enough.
	
		I wondered if his process helped create that sense of distance and conflict between your characters.	

	I think the blocking helped make that work — I was way up in the bleachers, and he was down there. That worked. In general, I was very adversarial with everybody in the room. I was interrupting the smooth speak they were giving Zuckerberg. I love all the dialogue Wunmi Mosaku has, where she tells him, “Don’t say humans.” It’s almost like being a defense attorney for an ax murderer, and you know he did it.

	All these years making fun of corporations, I’ve secretly always wanted to be in a conference room. How do they talk around the fact that they know there’s lead in their toothpaste? It reminded me of that movie “Zone of Interest.” When the Nazis are talking about the victims, they call them “cargo” or something. They can’t even say what they’re doing. I find that fascinating.
	
	
		Or like in “Succession,” when a low-level employee is abused they call it “NRPI”: No Real Person Involved.	

	The thing about these corporations is it’s nameless and faceless. The general public will get mad at a singer or a golfer or a comedian, and it’s like: “All right, buddy. Name the top 10 CEOs.” They can’t do it. But if you’re an individual who hoards hand sanitizer during a pandemic, everybody knows who you are and where you live.



	

					Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning”
									©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		I’ve heard you talk about these “nerds with apps” sort of ruining the country —	

	Not sort of! They are absolutely doing it. And they’re closing the door behind them and putting a tremendous amount of people out of work. Economically — forget environmentally — they’re leading us to ruin. When it’s just you making the money, how’s somebody going to buy the widget you’re making? Capitalism is great. Unregulated capitalism is frightening.
	
		You said recently that while preparing for a scene in “The Social Reckoning,” you got emotional to the point of tears. What made you so emotional? Did the material hit close to home?	

	It wasn’t the material. No, that was from being walled off emotionally. This has happened to me throughout my acting career. Occasionally I will get a scene, and if my character feels a feeling that is on the spectrum of vulnerable, I can all of a sudden well up like I’m at a funeral, and I never understood what it was. The way they raised boys to be men, you weren’t allowed to feel any of those feelings, so I have walled those off for so long that I don’t feel those feelings. And when I act, these characters do. So then I have to open the vault to go in there to get disappointed or whatever. And when I open the door, what happens is literally a cry from 40 years ago gets out.
	
		And the scene didn’t call for crying?	

	I forget what scene it was, but it didn’t call for crying. It’s bizarre. Instead of misdirected anger, it’s like misdirected crying. I had to cry this out by myself in a hotel room, and then the next day I was able to do the scene. I finally figured out why it was happening. When I act, all of a sudden I would just feel alive, and it was because I was opening that door that I had closed off for protection when I was a kid a long time ago.
	
	
		Were you worried you might not be able to execute the scene?	

	I was in a sheer panic that I was going to go to set and fall apart, and it would not have made sense. Because some people think if you’re acting and you’re crying, you must be doing a good job. Well, not if it doesn’t call for that. Then it’s weird.
	
		It’s fascinating that acting has had such a therapeutic effect on you.	

	Yeah, it does. I also have been doing these breathwork massages and have finally gotten rid of 90% of my childhood anger. I can say now that I’m not an angry person. I mean, I still can get angry, but it’s just another emotion. I’m not bringing my entire life experience with it, which is what I used to do. I used to walk around at an eight, and now I start at zero.

	It’s like in pickup sports, when everyone’s trying to have a good time and burn some calories, and there’s always that one person bringing Game 7 energy. And you’re like, “Come on, man! I’m not trying to get my knee blown out here. There are no scouts in the stands.” My anger was like that. And getting it all out is something I’m really dedicated to.

title: Ex-WWE Star Eva Marie Sells Pink Ring Gear, Proceeds Partially Going to Recovery
description:
Ex-WWE Star Eva Marie
                          Want My Ring Gear?! Come Get It!!!
body:
Ex-WWE Star Eva Marie
                          Want My Ring Gear?! Come Get It!!!
                      
      
    
            If you ever had your eye on Eva Marie's fun wrestling fits ... now's your chance to take 'em home!
      
    
            The ex-WWE star is auctioning off her iconic ring gear from when she faced off against Alexa Bliss during SummerSlam 2021.
      
    
            The wrestler is parting ways with her signature pink palette, metallic detailing, and gold wrestling boots, and she tells TMZ they're the real deal.
      

            Eva says ... "These aren't replicas. They're pieces I wore, competed in and have personally held onto because they represent such important moments in my career."
      
    
            The auction will be going down on her new Passes page, and 50% of the proceeds go to NEM Recovery Centers to help people struggling with alcohol and addiction.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She tells us the donation is important to her, explaining ... "Now, all these years later, I get to take something from my WWE career, the same career that gave me a platform to share my recovery story, and use it to help someone else find recovery."
      
    
            Eva says she also plans to use it to build a deeper connection with her fans, telling TMZ ... "I want my Passes to feel like you're actually hanging out with me -- not just watching my life through a perfectly edited Instagram post."
      
    
            According to Eva, the page won't be just memorabilia auctions ... it will also include BTS content from shoots, events, and workouts ... as well as content from WWE and her personal life she's never shared before.

title: Elon Musk Kicked Daughter Off Insurance After She Came Out as Trans, First Wife Says
description:
Elon Musk's First Wife
                          He Kicked Our Trans Daughter Off Insurance ... A
body:
Elon Musk's First Wife
                          He Kicked Our Trans Daughter Off Insurance ... After Saying He'd Always Love Her
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 9, 2026
                            5:54 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Elon Musk is revealing the way he treated his trans daughter behind closed doors during their public falling out ... according to his first wife.
      
    
            The billionaire's ex-wife, Justine Wilson, says in the upcoming "Musk" documentary that Elon treated Vivian Wilson's transition as the "death of a child."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She says Vivian was in "pain" when the X owner posted that he felt he'd lost her to the "woke mind virus."
      

            Justine said ... "Elon was telling her, through telling the world, what that point of view actually was. And Elon never tried to repair things, that’s not in his nature."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She also revealed that -- after Vivian came out as trans -- Elon told Justin to tell their daughter, "I’ll always love her" ... but then cut off Vivian's health insurance the next day.
      
    
            Vivian's had a rough relationship with Musk ever since -- she ditched his last name a few years back and recently appeared in a series of anti-A.I. ads where she said ... "Some things aren't meant to be fixed."

title: Pregnant Woman Found Dead in Burning Van, Still Alive When It Was Set on Fire
description:
Pregnant Woman Dead
                          Found in Burning Van ... 2 Men Arrested
body:
Pregnant Woman Dead
                          Found in Burning Van ... 2 Men Arrested
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Samantha Natalie Phythian was found dead inside a burning van in Wales and was apparently still alive and pregnant when someone set the vehicle on fire.
      
    
            According to the BBC, the judge said in a court hearing Friday ... "At the time of ignition the person was alive. Someone set the van alight and the person was alive and was killed as a result of the fire."
      
    
            38-year-old Thomas Bell -- who's been charged with Samantha's murder -- appeared in court on video.
      

            The court was told he knew Samantha, but denied setting the fire. After the hearing, police said they'd arrested a second man was arrested in connection with her death.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The unnamed 47-year-old was booked for suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson and possession with intent to supply drugs.
      
    
            On Friday, police also confirmed Samantha had been pregnant at the time of her death.
      
    
            She was found dead in the vehicle on Sunday, after emergency services were called for reports of a vehicle fire near an industrial estate and retail park around 11:30 PM that night.
      
    
            The judge in the case said Bell would be back in court for a plea and preparation hearing at the end of November.
      
    
            A provisional date for the trial has been set for the beginning of April 2027.

title: Sam Altman Ripped By Suicide Victim's Mother After ChatGPT Helped Edit Suicide Notes
description:
Sam Altman
                          Suicide Victim's Mom Slams Him ...
body:
Sam Altman
                          Suicide Victim's Mom Slams Him ...
                          After ChatGPT Edited Note
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A mother whose daughter used ChatGPT to write her suicide notes heard Sam Altman's response ... and she's not happy with the OpenAI honcho.
      
    
            Journalist Laura Reiley says Altman taking "the privacy high road" in refusing to turn over potentially insightful chat logs is "a little rich."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            She called out the hypocrisy of Altman's OpenAI and other tech companies earning revenue from advertising strategies that involve users' personal information.
      

            Laura also argues it's either "disingenuous or misinformed" for Altman to claim that experts aren't sure what to do, writing ... "Researchers have been saying loud and clear: We need user data and chatbot interactions to conduct research."
      
    
            She says she would gladly hand over her late daughter Sophie's chat log if it meant it could help researchers determine "what pushes someone from vague suicidal ideation to executing on a suicide plan."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            But when the potential solution was recently floated to Altman, he argued that it would be a violation of privacy to access someone's private chat logs.
      
    
            Laura even asked ChatGPT what it thought of Sophie relying on the A.I. chatbot as a makeshift therapist.
      
    
            It said ... "Having access to good therapeutic language is not the same as possessing reliable clinical judgment in a live, unfolding crisis."
      
    
            Laura took one last dig at Altman ... "I'm not sure I've heard a human explain AI's chief shortcoming so succinctly."
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.
